---
title: "Penalizing in-sample fit"
---

The [likelihood-ratio page](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) fixed a Provo position table and two nested Gaussian mean models. Information criteria use those same likelihoods but replace null-hypothesis calibration with a penalty for estimated flexibility. This lets the penalty, rather than a change in data or response, explain any disagreement.

The [**optimism of training error**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) is the fact that performance on observations used for fitting tends to be better than expected performance on new observations. An [**information criterion**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) estimates a correction by combining fitted likelihood with a complexity penalty. Its score is relative to compatible candidates; the absolute value has no standalone linguistic unit.

The [Provo dossier](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd#provo-measurement-dossier) reminds us
that one likelihood contribution is an aggregated content-word position. Its mean
log FFD averages logged reader fixations, and positions remain grouped within 55
passages. Those facts determine what the criteria can approximate.

We first derive the distinct penalties used by AIC and BIC, then observe their disagreement on the fixed Provo comparison, and finally identify the response, observation unit, and sampling assumptions that neither criterion can choose for us.

## Information criteria compared {#information-criteria-compared}

## AIC: fit plus a parameter-count penalty

Let $\ell$ be maximized log likelihood and $k$ the number of likelihood parameters. The [**Akaike information criterion (AIC)**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) is

$$
\operatorname{AIC}=2k-2\ell
=
\underbrace{-2\ell}_{\text{lack of fitted likelihood}}
+
\underbrace{2k}_{\text{complexity penalty}}.
$$

Greater maximized log likelihood lowers the first term; additional parameters increase the second. Lower AIC is preferred. The penalty is motivated as an approximation to relative expected predictive discrepancy, not as a significance threshold.

The factor 2 can be motivated by a local expansion. Under a regular correctly
specified model, the maximum-likelihood estimate varies approximately as

$$
\widehat\theta-\theta_0
\ \dot\sim\
\operatorname{Normal}\left(0,\frac{1}{n}I(\theta_0)^{-1}\right).
$$

A second-order expansion of new-data log likelihood around $\theta_0$ contains the
quadratic term

$$
n(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)^T I(\theta_0)
(\widehat\theta-\theta_0).
$$

Its expectation is

$$
\operatorname{tr}\left[
nI(\theta_0)\frac{I(\theta_0)^{-1}}{n}
\right]
=\operatorname{tr}(I_k)=k.
$$

Fitting and evaluating on the same observations gains about $k$ log-likelihood
units relative to evaluation on new observations. On the $-2\ell$ scale, correcting
that optimism adds approximately $2k$. This argument depends on a regular,
identified likelihood and an effective observation unit compatible with its
information calculation.

## BIC: a different penalty and motivation

The [**Bayesian information criterion (BIC)**](https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf) is

$$
\operatorname{BIC}=k\log n-2\ell,
$$

where $n$ is the sample size supplied to the approximation. Its penalty grows with $\log n$. BIC is not merely a universally stricter AIC: it arises from a different approximation connected to model evidence under additional assumptions.

Begin with the marginal likelihood for model $M$:

$$
p(y\mid M)=\int L(\theta;y)\pi(\theta\mid M)\,\mathrm d\theta.
$$

A Laplace approximation expands the log integrand around its interior mode. If the
observed information grows like $nI(\widehat\theta)$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log p(y\mid M)
&\approx
\ell(\widehat\theta)
+\log\pi(\widehat\theta)
+\frac{k}{2}\log(2\pi)
-\frac12\log|nI(\widehat\theta)|\\
&=
\ell(\widehat\theta)-\frac{k}{2}\log n+O(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying by $-2$ and dropping candidate-specific terms treated as bounded gives
$-2\ell+k\log n$. This approximation assumes, among other things, identifiable
regular parameters, a locally positive smooth prior, and an information scale that
really grows with the declared $n$.

Repeated linguistic data can make the meaning of $n$ delicate. The Provo teaching table contains position summaries rather than reader-level observations, so its criterion calculation uses the number of retained positions. It cannot convert those positions into independent readers or passages.

## The Provo criterion disagreement

The code reloads the [Provo table introduced on the preceding page](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd#provo-measurement-dossier), refits the identical linear and quadratic models, and computes both criteria. The likelihood parameter count returned by `logLik()` includes the residual scale parameter.

The bookkeeping differs from the grouping structure:

| model | mean coefficients | likelihood parameters | grouping units retained in the table |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| linear | 2 | 3, including residual scale | positions nested within 55 passages | <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
| quadratic | 3 | 4, including residual scale | positions nested within 55 passages | <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

Thus the calculation uses $n=1{,}593$ position summaries because those are the rows
whose Gaussian densities are multiplied. It does not claim that 1,593 independent
passages or readers were observed. Dependence among positions makes the usual
large-sample motivation questionable even when the software calculation is exact.

```{r}
#| label: provo-information-criteria
#| message: false
#| warning: false

provo <- utils::read.csv(
  "data/provo/content-word-positions.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
provo$cloze_surprisal_bits <- -log2(provo$OrthoMatchModel)

linear_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits,
  data = provo
)
quadratic_fit <- lm(
  mean_log_ffd ~ cloze_surprisal_bits + I(cloze_surprisal_bits^2),
  data = provo
)
stopifnot(identical(
  rownames(model.frame(linear_fit)),
  rownames(model.frame(quadratic_fit))
))

criteria <- data.frame(
  model = c("Linear", "Quadratic"),
  n_positions = nrow(provo),
  mean_parameters = c(
    length(coef(linear_fit)), length(coef(quadratic_fit))
  ),
  likelihood_parameters = c(
    attr(logLik(linear_fit), "df"),
    attr(logLik(quadratic_fit), "df")
  ),
  log_likelihood = c(
    as.numeric(logLik(linear_fit)),
    as.numeric(logLik(quadratic_fit))
  ),
  aic = c(AIC(linear_fit), AIC(quadratic_fit)),
  bic = c(BIC(linear_fit), BIC(quadratic_fit))
)
criteria$delta_aic <- criteria$aic - min(criteria$aic)
criteria$delta_bic <- criteria$bic - min(criteria$bic)
criteria

criterion_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    model = criteria$model,
    criterion = "AIC",
    difference_from_best = criteria$delta_aic
  ),
  data.frame(
    model = criteria$model,
    criterion = "BIC",
    difference_from_best = criteria$delta_bic
  )
)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  criterion_plot,
  ggplot2::aes(model, difference_from_best)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2, color = "#2B6CB0") +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ criterion, scales = "free_y") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Difference from preferred score"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

Both criteria use the same `r format(nrow(provo), big.mark = ",")` position summaries. AIC prefers the `r criteria$model[which.min(criteria$aic)]` model; the other model is worse by `r sprintf("%.3f", max(criteria$delta_aic))` AIC points. BIC prefers the `r criteria$model[which.min(criteria$bic)]` model; the other model is worse by `r sprintf("%.3f", max(criteria$delta_bic))` BIC points. The empirical disagreement follows from applying different penalties to a modest fitted-likelihood gain.

In the code, `log_likelihood` is $\ell$, `likelihood_parameters` is $k$, and
`n_positions` is the supplied $n$. `AIC()` computes $-2\ell+2k`; `BIC()` computes
$-2\ell+k\log n`; and subtracting each column minimum produces the plotted relative
differences. The table is thus the numerical crosswalk for every term in both
criteria.

This is more informative than declaring either criterion decisive. The candidates are close enough that a defensible change in approximation can reverse the ordering. The plot shows only each model's distance from the preferred score; it does not add thresholds or labels that the criteria do not supply.

## Keeping responses and observations fixed

Information criteria compare models only when their likelihoods concern the same observed responses. A model of raw duration and a model of log duration assign density to different response variables. Their printed values are not directly comparable without accounting for the transformation.

Candidate models can also silently use different rows when an added predictor has missing values. The code thus checks the row names in both model frames. Equal row counts alone would not establish that the same positions were used.

## What the criteria do not encode

AIC approximates observation-level expected performance under its regularity conditions. It does not create held-out predictions or know which linguistic group should be new. BIC likewise cannot distinguish another position in an observed passage from a position in a passage absent during fitting.

The position count also does not license reader-level or passage-level inference. Direct grouped validation is preferable when prediction for a wholly new passage is the target. Here the criteria compare two compatible likelihood models for the fixed aggregated position table.

An information-criterion difference is not a conventional significance threshold. It ranks specified candidates under its approximation. It does not certify that the preferred candidate is an adequate explanation of the response process.

## Checking the penalized comparison

1. Which term rewards fitted likelihood in AIC, and which term penalizes flexibility?
2. Why can AIC and BIC prefer different Provo models while using identical fits?
3. Why must both candidates use the same response rows and response scale?
4. Which held-out unit is not represented by either criterion calculation?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $-2\ell$ rewards fitted likelihood and $2k$ penalizes estimated flexibility.
2. AIC adds $2k$, while BIC adds $k\log n$ under a different approximation.
3. Otherwise a score difference would mix the candidate-model difference with a
   change in the modeled observations.
4. Neither calculation directly omits a complete passage or reader.

</details>

## Recap and forward link

1. AIC corrects regular training-fit optimism by approximately $2k$.
2. BIC uses a Laplace approximation with penalty $k\log n$.
3. The Provo $n$ is the number of aggregated position rows, not the number of
   independent passages.

The [previous page](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd#provo-measurement-dossier)
calibrated the nested restriction; the [next page](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd#normal-inverse-gamma-posterior-and-predictive-update)
obtains exact omitted-position predictions under a fixed Bayesian specification.
